claims.claim: yellow perch hatch at 5.6–6.2 mm in Lake Itasca (Whiteside, Swindoll & Doolittle 1985)
claims.note: article not read. Stand-in (Swindoll 1981 thesis, same lake and programme): perch 'hatched in the littoral zone at 5.5-6.0 mm total length' (thesis abstract); first littoral fry averaged 6 mm (range 5.8–6.2) on 26 May 1979 and 5.8 mm (5.7–5.9) on 6 May 1980 (Results, pp. 21–22). The 5.6–6.2 mm range itself was not seen in any text read

claims.claim: yellow perch larvae move offshore soon after hatching, 'probably a mechanism to escape intense predation in the littoral zone' (Whiteside, Swindoll & Doolittle 1985, abstract)
claims.note: article and abstract not read. Stand-in (Swindoll 1981): within two weeks of hatching all fry moved into the limnetic zone and stayed there until ~25 mm, then returned inshore (abstract; Results pp. 21–22: fry left the littoral 12–13 days after hatching); the Discussion (pp. 43–44) concludes 'the most probable explanation for the initial, offshore migration of perch fry is that they do so to escape predation'

notes: Needs the article (Springer, doi:10.1007/BF00007709, via a library login). Stand-in read in full: Swindoll, C. M. 1981. The growth, diet and distribution of yellow perch fry, Perca flavescens, in Lake Itasca, Minnesota. MS thesis, University of Tennessee, Knoxville (TRACE: https://trace.tennessee.edu/bitstreams/181a1342-4d08-44c9-b0d5-1883fb5cfd21/download). It supports the offshore move and its predation interpretation (pp. 21–22, 43–44) and gives hatch length 5.5–6.0 mm TL; it could be cited for these instead of the abstract. Note it also says fry 'first fed at 9-10 mm' in Lake Itasca (abstract), which sits against Table 3.6-1's 'first feeding at 5.6 mm, 2.4 mg' (whatever that row's source is); and growth ~0.50 mm/d for the first 40 days, ~0.43 mm/d after; first food copepod nauplii, copepodids and rotifers, cladocerans from 20–24 mm. Spawning about a week after ice-off; hatch at 11–12 °C (1979) and 18.5–19.5 °C (1980).
